title: Gold in rags
hook: Buddha-nature like gold wrapped in dirty rags, or honey guarded by bees (Tathagatagarbha Sutra)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Avalokiteshvara in the Surangama, listening, then listening to listening. Your line: turn the hearing around. Did one sound become a bell for you? Day one thousand two hundred three.

A lump of baked clay sits on a workshop floor. It's black from the furnace, cracked, ugly, the kind of thing you'd sweep out with the ashes. A smith picks it up, turns it over, and taps it with a hammer. The clay falls away in pieces. Inside is a statue of the Buddha, cast in gold. The mold was never the point. It was only what the gold was poured into. That picture sits in a short Mahayana sutra, the Tathagatagarbha, alongside another: a golden statue wrapped in filthy rags. Today: gold in rags.
screen: `A BLACKENED LUMP OF CLAY.` → `ONE TAP OF THE HAMMER.` → `GOLD INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Back on day eleven hundred two, this path met the teaching itself: every living being carries Buddha-nature, covered but never lost. Today, a closer look at how the sutra paints it, and what the pictures ask of the one looking. First, the rags. A traveler carries a golden statue through rough country and dies on the road. The statue, wrapped in rotten cloth, lies in the dirt. People step over it. Nobody passing by sees what it is. Someone with clear eyes has to see it and have it unwrapped. Second, the bees. Honey hangs in a tree, and a swarm guards it. Someone who wants the honey doesn't attack the honey. They find a skillful way past the bees. Third, the house. A poor family lives over a buried treasure. The treasure can't speak up and say, I'm here. So they stay poor, standing on gold. Fourth, the woman. A poor, lonely woman, looked down on by everyone, is carrying a child who will become a king. She doesn't know it. She thinks of herself the way the street thinks of her. Lay the pictures side by side and a pattern shows. In each one, the covering is real: rags rot, bees sting, poverty hurts. And in each one, the treasure can't announce itself. Someone has to see past the covering, and the sutra says that's what a Buddha does, looking at beings and seeing what they carry. And the pictures keep showing the ones who walk past. The rags don't make the statue less gold, but they make it very easy to step over.
screen: `THE STATUE IN THE RAGS.` · `THE HONEY AND THE BEES.` · `TREASURE UNDER A POOR HOUSE.` · `A POOR WOMAN CARRYING A KING.` · then, large: `THE TREASURE CAN'T SPEAK UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: see gold in one rough person. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind someone whose rags are obvious to you. Rude, careless, worn out, hard to like. Don't pretend the rags aren't there. Just notice them, plainly. Then, gently, look past them, the way the smith looks at the clay. Somewhere in there is the gold the sutra talks about. You don't need to see it clearly. Only allow that it might be there. The bell holds the time.
Gold in rags. In the Tathagatagarbha Sutra, a golden Buddha statue wrapped in filthy cloth: a picture of Buddha-nature, covered but never lost. Today's word.
Your line: gold in the rags. Today, when someone is easy to step over, slow down for one second, the way you would for something dropped on the road. Day one thousand two hundred three.

howItsDone: In East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism, the similes of the Tathagatagarbha Sutra are used in teaching about Buddha-nature, and teachers point to them when encouraging respect for every being.

match.prompt: the pictures in the sutra: tap the pairs.
pairs: wrapped in rotten rags on the road
guarded by a swarm of bees

myth: in the sutra, the treasure under the house tells the family it's there
the treasure can't speak. the family stays poor, standing on gold.
in the pictures, the coverings are harmless
rags rot, bees sting, poverty hurts. the covering is real, but it isn't the treasure.
the sutra says a Buddha looks at beings and sees what they carry
like the one with clear eyes who unwraps the statue.

fork.setup: you're a smith. on the floor is a cracked, blackened lump of clay, fresh from the furnace. what do you do with it?
options: sweep it out with the ashes
break it open with a hammer
polish the outside of the clay
fork.reveal: the smith taps it open, and inside is a golden Buddha. in the sutra the mold is the covering, and the gold was there all along.

trapdoor: what you thought: gold in rags means hidden potential.
what it means: a golden statue nobody sees because of its wrapping, a picture of Buddha-nature in every being.
what a scholar hears: the Tathagatagarbha Sutra teaches by a string of pictures, and in each one the treasure can't announce itself.
recall: a householder of Vaishali, not a monk
hears it secondhand, and is glad

sources.ref: Tathagatagarbha Sutra, the similes (statue in rags, honey and bees, treasure under a poor house, poor woman carrying a future king, gold statue in a clay mold)

notes: All paraphrase. Day 1102 already used gold in filth, honey, husk and the statue in rags; this day leads with the clay mold and gives most time to the poor house and the poor woman to avoid repeating.

Check details of the similes: the traveler dying on the road with the statue; spirits/devas not seeing it; the treasure 'cannot speak'; the woman not knowing she carries a future king; the smith breaking the mold.
Check the statement that the sutra presents a Buddha as seeing the hidden nature in beings.
The index hook says 'gold wrapped in dirty rags'; in the sutra the wrapped object is a golden Buddha statue. Written as a golden statue.

Editor pass: cut 'still warm' from the mold (the sutra has the mold cool before it is broken); cut the unsourced 'better-known'; replaced 'even the spirits can't see it' (in the sutra a deva with the divine eye does see it and has it unwrapped) with 'nobody passing by sees what it is'; softened 'who the pictures are hardest on' to a plain observation.
